`brsmm()` adds Gaussian random effects to the mean submodel of `brs()`
for clustered or longitudinal scores (patients with repeated visits,
raters, centers). This vignette covers the model, the integration methods,
random-effect summaries and tests, marginal and conditional predictions,
residuals, group-level cross-validation and simulation. The
interval-censored likelihood and the interval maps are those of
`vignette("brs-intro")`. The data sets are small so that the vignette
builds quickly; the results are illustrative.

```{r library}
library(betaregscale)
```

## The model

For observation $i$ of group $g$,
$$
g_1(\mu_{gi}) = x_{gi}^\top \beta + w_{gi}^\top b_g, \qquad
g_2(\sigma_{gi}) = z_{gi}^\top \gamma, \qquad b_g \sim N(0, D),
$$
where $w_{gi}$ is the row of the random-effects design given by
`random = ~ terms | group` (`~ 1 | id` for a random intercept,
`~ 1 + x | id` for an intercept and a slope with a free correlation). The
dispersion submodel has no random effects. Given $b_g$, each score
contributes the cell probability of `brs()`, and the marginal
log-likelihood is
$$
\ell(\theta) = \sum_g \log \int \prod_i P(S_{gi} = s_{gi} \mid b)\,
\varphi(b; 0, D)\, db .
$$
$D = LL^\top$ is parameterized by its lower Cholesky factor: the log of
each diagonal entry and the off-diagonal entries. These are the
`(re_chol_logsd)_` and `(re_chol)_` entries of `coef()`; for a random
intercept the single entry is $\log \mathrm{SD}(b)$.

## Integration methods

The integral is computed around the mode $\hat b_g$ of the log integrand,
with curvature $H_g$ there:

- `int_method = "laplace"` (default): the Laplace approximation, fast and
  accurate when groups are not tiny.
- `int_method = "aghq"`: adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature with `n_points`
  nodes per dimension (default 11) on a product grid centered at $\hat b_g$
  and scaled by $H_g^{-1/2}$ (at most 500000 nodes).
- `int_method = "qmc"`: importance sampling from $N(\hat b_g, H_g^{-1})$
  on `qmc_points` Halton points (default 1024). It is deterministic and,
  with two or more random effects, slightly underestimates the
  log-likelihood; prefer `"aghq"` for up to three random effects.

`optim()` uses the compiled gradient of the chosen approximation; the
Hessian for `vcov()` is a central difference of that gradient.

## Simulated data

`brsmm_sim()` simulates scores from this model, given the random-effect
standard deviations and correlation. Here: 30 patients with four visits on
an NRS-11 scale, a centered time `tc`, a treatment arm `trt`, and a random
intercept and time slope:

```{r sim}
d <- expand.grid(visit = 1:4, id = 1:30)
d$tc <- (d$visit - 2.5) / 1.5
d$trt <- as.integer(d$id %% 2 == 0)
set.seed(7)
s <- brsmm_sim(~ tc + trt, random = ~ 1 + tc | id, data = d,
               beta = c(-0.3, -0.4, -0.5), phi = qlogis(0.15),
               re_sd = c(0.8, 0.3), re_cor = 0.3, ncuts = 10)
head(s)
attr(s, "truth")$par
```

The attribute `"truth"` holds the true parameters in the order and on the
scale of `coef()`, and `"ranef"` the simulated random effects.

## Fitting

```{r fit}
fit_ri <- brsmm(y ~ tc + trt, random = ~ 1 | id, data = s)
fit_rs <- brsmm(y ~ tc + trt, random = ~ 1 + tc | id, data = s)
summary(fit_rs)
```

The random-effects block reports the standard deviations and the
correlation with intervals built on the log scale (SD) and the
$\mathrm{atanh}$ scale (correlation) and mapped back. It gives no $z$-test:
a variance of zero lies on the boundary of the parameter space, so test it
with `anova()` (below). The same numbers are in `summary(fit)$varcorr`.

The three integration methods give nearly the same estimates on this data:

```{r methods}
fit_aghq <- brsmm(y ~ tc + trt, random = ~ 1 | id, data = s,
                  int_method = "aghq", n_points = 7)
fit_qmc <- brsmm(y ~ tc + trt, random = ~ 1 | id, data = s,
                 int_method = "qmc", qmc_points = 256)
round(cbind(laplace = c(coef(fit_ri), logLik = logLik(fit_ri)),
            aghq = c(coef(fit_aghq), logLik = logLik(fit_aghq)),
            qmc = c(coef(fit_qmc), logLik = logLik(fit_qmc))), 4)
```

## Random effects

`ranef()` returns the conditional modes $\hat b_g$, one row per group;
`fit$random$D` and `fit$random$sd_b` hold the estimated covariance matrix
and standard deviations:

```{r ranef}
head(ranef(fit_rs))
fit_rs$random$D
```

`brsmm_re_study()` summarizes the random effects: the covariance, the
shrinkage of the modes and the intraclass correlation of
$\mathrm{logit}(Y)$, computed with the beta level-1 variance:

```{r re-study}
brsmm_re_study(fit_rs)
```

```{r re-plot, fig.height = 4}
autoplot.brsmm(fit_rs, type = "ranef_caterpillar")
```

`autoplot.brsmm()` also draws `"ranef_density"`, `"ranef_pairs"`,
`"ranef_qq"`, `"shrinkage"`, `"calibration"`, `"score_dist"` and
`"residuals_by_group"`; `plot.brsmm()` gives the panels of `plot.brs()`
with response or Pearson residuals, plus random-effect panels.

## Testing variance components

Adding a random-effect term puts its variance on the boundary of the
parameter space under the null hypothesis, so the likelihood ratio does
not follow $\chi^2_d$. When a model adds one random-effect term,
`anova()` uses the mixture $\frac12\chi^2_{d-1} + \frac12\chi^2_d$
(Self and Liang, 1987; Stram and Lee, 1994): $\frac12\chi^2_0 +
\frac12\chi^2_1$ from `brs()` to a random intercept, and
$\frac12\chi^2_1 + \frac12\chi^2_2$ from a random intercept to an
intercept and slope. The heading of the table says which rows use it.

```{r anova}
fit_0 <- brs(y ~ tc + trt, data = s)
anova(fit_0, fit_ri, fit_rs)
```

When a variance is essentially zero, `brsmm()` warns "Variance component
at the boundary"; rely on the likelihood-ratio test for that term.

`BIC()` accepts several fits and returns a table, as `stats::BIC()`
does (`AIC()` takes one fit; `brs_table()` compares several). There is no
single sample size for a mixed model: `BIC()` counts observations by
default and groups with `n = "groups"`. Compare BIC values only under the
same convention.

```{r ic}
BIC(fit_ri, fit_rs)
BIC(fit_ri, fit_rs, n = "groups")
```

## Conditional and marginal predictions

`predict()` gives conditional quantities: a group of the fit uses its mode
$\hat b_g$, a new group gets $b = 0$:

```{r predict}
nd <- data.frame(tc = 0, trt = 1, id = c(1, 999))
predict(fit_ri, newdata = nd, type = "expected_score")
```

Under a nonlinear link, the prediction at $b = 0$ describes a subject whose
random effects are zero, which is not the population average.
`brs_marginal()` integrates the random effects out to give
population-averaged score probabilities, expected scores and exceedance
probabilities $P(S \ge k)$, with delta-method standard errors over all
parameters; `conditional = TRUE` sets $b = 0$ instead. The grouping
variable is not needed in `newdata`:

```{r marginal}
nd <- data.frame(tc = c(-1, 1), trt = 1)
brs_marginal(fit_ri, nd, type = "expected_score")
brs_marginal(fit_ri, nd, type = "expected_score", conditional = TRUE)
```

Differences between rows, such as the change from the first to the last
visit in $P(S \ge 5)$, are given by `contrast`:

```{r marginal-contrast}
brs_marginal(fit_ri, nd, type = "exceed", k = 5, contrast = c(2, 1))
```

## Residuals

For `type = "rqr"` (randomized quantile residuals) and `"cell_deviance"`,
`re` selects how the random effects enter:

- `"conditional"` (default): at the modes $\hat b_g$. The modes are shrunk
  toward zero, so these residuals are not exactly $N(0, 1)$ under the
  model, especially for small groups.
- `"marginal"`: from the marginal distribution of each observation, with
  the random effects integrated out. Each residual is $N(0, 1)$ under the
  model; residuals of the same group are correlated.
- `"posterior"`: at one draw of each $b_g$ from its posterior (importance
  resampling with `n_draws` proposals per group, default 200). These are
  close to independent $N(0, 1)$ under the model, without the shrinkage of
  the modes.

```{r residuals}
set.seed(1)
res <- sapply(c("conditional", "marginal", "posterior"), function(r)
  residuals(fit_ri, type = "rqr", re = r))
round(rbind(mean = colMeans(res), sd = apply(res, 2, sd)), 3)
```

The other types of `residuals.brs()` (`"response"`, `"pearson"`, ...) are
evaluated at the conditional modes.

## Group-level cross-validation

`brsmm_cv()` forms folds by group, so all observations of a group are held
out together. Each held-out group is scored by its marginal
log-likelihood at the training estimates: its random effects are
integrated out, so no estimate of them is needed. `seed` makes the folds
reproducible, and `attr(, "folds")` returns them for reuse with another
model:

```{r cv}
cv_ri <- brsmm_cv(y ~ tc + trt, random = ~ 1 | id, data = s, k = 3, seed = 1)
cv_ri
folds <- attr(cv_ri, "folds")[[1]]
cv_rs <- brsmm_cv(y ~ tc + trt, random = ~ 1 + tc | id, data = s,
                  folds = folds)
c(ri = attr(cv_ri, "log_score"), rs = attr(cv_rs, "log_score"))
```

The total held-out log score is the log probability of the held-out
scores (higher is better). For score data it is on the same scale as the
held-out log-likelihood of any other model that gives a pmf on
$0, \ldots, K$, evaluated on the same folds. `brs_loglik_contrib()` returns
the per-group contributions of a fit, also for new data.

## Simulation from a fit

`simulate()` draws new scores from a fitted model. For `brsmm` fits,
`re = "marginal"` (default) draws new random effects and
`re = "conditional"` keeps the conditional modes. A quick check compares
the observed share of each border score with its simulated distribution:

```{r simulate}
sims <- simulate(fit_ri, nsim = 50, seed = 1)
obs <- c(p0 = mean(s$y == 0), p10 = mean(s$y == 10))
sim_p <- rbind(p0 = colMeans(sims == 0), p10 = colMeans(sims == 10))
cbind(observed = obs, t(apply(sim_p, 1, quantile, c(0.05, 0.95))))
```

## Boundary cutpoints

`cutpoints = "boundary"` works in `brsmm()` as in `brs()` (see
`vignette("brs-intro")`), with the same requirements and the same 2-df
likelihood-ratio test against the fixed map; `brsmm_sim()` simulates from
given boundary cutpoints.
